title: acme-churn: what relates to 60-day churn, and what to fix first
subtitle: Exploration of data/snapshots.csv before any split. Nothing in the repository was changed.

verdict.text: Not ready to split. First re-run the extract so the 1,587 unfinished rows get real labels (or drop them), then remove `retention_call_outcome` and find out what changed in November 2025.

stats.label: Features with signal
stats.note: one of them is the leak

sections.title: What we found
sections.intro: Feature measures use the 4,413 rows dated through 2026-01-31, without the personal columns. The over-time view uses all 6,000.

items.title: `retention_call_outcome` is the outcome itself
items.evidence: Filled on exactly the 665 positive rows and blank on all 5,335 negative rows. Strength 1.000 on its own.
items.fix: Remove it before any split. It records what happened after the customer was already leaving.

items.title: 1,587 rows (26%) have labels that are not finished
items.evidence: Rate 7.6% on those rows against 19.0% in January 2026. By month: February 16.0%, March 8.1%, April 0.65%. At an assumed extract on 2026-04-01 the windows are 59, 31 and 0 of the 60 days. [med] The March and April rates fit an extract within a few days of 1 April. Each of these rows is labelled no only because the answer is not in yet.
items.fix: Best: run the extract again. Today is 2026-11-10, so snapshots through 2026-09-01 can have a complete window, which would also add labelled months after the step below. Otherwise drop them, and keep February only if the extract is confirmed to be 2026-04-02 or later.

items.title: Churn stepped up in November 2025 and the table does not say why
items.evidence: 10.2% from January to October 2025 (3,246 rows) and 18.3% from November 2025 to January 2026 (1,167 rows). Chi-square across the 13 labelled months p 2.8e-08 (rows treated as independent). Without customers' earlier rows the step is still there, 14.9% to 23.9%. Plan, region, fee, logins, tickets and tenure do not shift, and all four plans rise: basic 10.3% to 16.8%, plus 8.3% to 17.4%, pro 11.3% to 16.4%, legacy 14.2% to 28.5%. The file holds one winter only: January rose year on year (13.5% to 24.3% without earlier rows), February did not (19.5% to 20.5%).
items.fix: Ask the business what changed around 1 November 2025: price, product, billing, or the definition of a cancellation. Until then treat older rows as a different base rate. Do not calibrate on the pooled rate.

items.title: The committed split and feature list would put these problems back
items.evidence: `split.py` cuts at 2026-04-01: on this table the test set would be the 612 April rows with 4 positives, and training would include 975 unfinished February and March rows. `features.py` lists `cancellation_reason`, which exists only after a cancellation, and `days_since_last_login`, which `extract.py` builds from the latest login ever with no limit at the snapshot date. `extract.py` also joins NPS with no as-of date.
items.fix: Do not reuse those three as they stand. Replace the split with the one under What to try, and leave both leaking columns out of the feature list.

items.title: The strongest usable signal is a blank `nps_last`, and the field does not behave like its name
items.evidence: On labelled rows churn is 43.2% when blank (653 rows) and 7.0% when filled. Strength 0.711, all of it from whether the value is present: the score itself is flat (rank strength 0.518). A blank alone flags 51.7% of churners at 43.2% precision, which meets the brief's bar. [med] It is not simply erased at cancellation: April rows, where almost nothing had happened yet, are already 18.0% blank, about what the blend of churners (50 to 55% blank) and non-churners (about 10%) gives. But 214 of the 1,354 customers with a score on their earlier row have a blank on the later one, which a true last score could not do, and later-row churn after that change is 45.3% against 9.7% when the score stays.
items.fix: Ask the owner how the field is filled and what makes it blank. Use a missing flag, not the score, and only once it is confirmed to be known at the snapshot date.

items.title: How rows were picked is unknown, and it changes the base rate
items.evidence: 1,295 labelled rows are a customer's earlier row of two and none of them is positive. The other rows are 17.5% positive, 545 of 3,118, against 12.35% for all labelled rows. Most of those zeros are natural: a customer present more than 60 days later cannot have churned. But for 181 pairs one month apart a positive is possible, roughly 15 would be expected, and none occurs. [med] The sample seems to depend on the outcome. The file also has 272 to 612 rows a month against about 40,000 active subscribers in the brief. Features do not separate these rows: logins, tickets, session length and fee have about the same mean as other non-churners.
items.fix: Ask how customers and dates were sampled. Keep the earlier rows, because dropping them would select on the future. Do not take a base rate for thresholds from this file until the sampling is known.

items.title: 1,500 of 4,500 customers have two rows
items.evidence: 3,000 rows belong to customers who appear twice, 1 to 15 months apart. A random split would put the same customer on both sides.
items.fix: Split by time and keep each customer on one side.

items.title: `avg_session_min` has a U shape that a linear term cannot see
items.evidence: Churn is 27.3% at 8 minutes or less, 4.5% at 20 to 22 minutes and 28.3% above 32 minutes. Strength from bins 0.663, from ranks 0.501. The shape is in both periods, and the column has no known source (see below).
items.fix: Use bins, the distance from about 20 minutes, or trees. Find out how it is computed before relying on the high end.

items.title: `tenure_months` uses 999 for unknown
items.evidence: 999 on 180 rows (3.0%), 143 of them labelled. Churn there is 10.5% (6.5% to 16.6%) against 12.4% elsewhere, so unknown does not behave differently. The next highest real value is 58.
items.fix: Replace 999 with a missing value before any transform. A separate flag is not needed.

items.title: Several columns have no known source
items.where: avg_session_min, campaign_code, is_internal_account, account_manager, annual_fee_eur, retention_call_outcome
items.evidence: These six are in the file but not in `model/extract.py`. So `snapshots.csv` comes from some other query, and it lacks three columns of the feature list (`payment_failures_90d`, `cancellation_reason`, `days_since_last_login`).
items.fix: Find the query that built this file. Without it nobody can say when those columns were known.

items.title: Some customer attributes change on almost every row
items.evidence: For the 1,500 customers with two rows the plan never changes, yet the fee differs on 1,493 (median 5.6%). The account manager matches on 280 and the discount on 304, about what chance gives with 6 and 5 levels. `campaign_code` matches on 2. None of them shows any signal.
items.fix: Ask whether these are really as of the snapshot. Leave them out unless a reason appears.

items.title: `annual_fee_eur` is 12 times `monthly_fee_eur`
items.evidence: Equal to within a cent on all 6,000 rows. Each fee also largely repeats plan (0.95).
items.fix: Drop the annual fee. Neither fee shows signal on its own.

items.title: Internal accounts are in the table
items.evidence: 29 rows, 22 labelled. Churn looks higher (22.7% labelled) but the group is too small to test after correction. The flag flips between the two rows of 18 customers.
items.fix: Exclude them from training, as they are not customers. Ask what the flag means, given the flips.

items.title: `campaign_code` has 400 levels and no signal
items.evidence: Every level has 4 to 26 rows, so none can be tested. Strength 0.504 on labelled rows.
items.fix: Leave it out, or group by campaign type if one exists.

items.title: Cleared: no duplicates
items.evidence: `snapshot_id` and (`customer_id`, `snapshot_date`) are each unique, and no two rows match on all other columns.

items.title: Cleared: the step is not a change of mix
items.where: plan, region, fee, logins, tickets, tenure
items.evidence: Means and shares are flat across the step, and the rate rises inside every plan. Feature strengths hold in both periods.
items.fix: Nothing to do on the mix. The cause remains open.

items.title: Cleared: `tenure_months` is consistent over time
items.evidence: Across two rows of one customer it grows by exactly the months elapsed in all 1,414 pairs without a 999.

items.title: Cleared: this table does not overlap the existing train and test files
items.evidence: Compared on keys only: no shared customer or snapshot. Those files have other columns and 3,400 rows. [med] That is the row count the brief quotes, so the brief's figures describe those files and not this table.
items.fix: Their holdout was not touched by this exploration.

blocks.text: Everything still open here should go through `ds-dataset` once a split exists.

items: [high] Remove `retention_call_outcome` before any split.
[high] Train only on rows with a complete 60-day window: snapshots through 2026-01-01 today, or a fresh extract with snapshots through 2026-09-01.
[high] Split forward in time with at least 60 days between the last training snapshot and the first test snapshot, and keep each customer on one side.

[med] With this file as it is, the split that fits is training through 2025-09-01 and test on 2025-11-01 to 2026-01-01. That is a hard test because the step falls between them, so it tells you whether the ranking survives, not whether the probabilities do.
[med] Try first: `logins_30d`, `tickets_90d`, `avg_session_min` and a legacy-plan flag. All hold their strength on both sides of the step.
[med] Add a blank flag for `nps_last` only after the owner confirms when it is set. Use the flag, not the score.
[high] Give `avg_session_min` bins or a squared distance from about 20 minutes, or use trees. A linear term sees nothing.
[high] Replace 999 in `tenure_months` with a missing value and drop `annual_fee_eur`.
[high] Drop internal accounts and the three personal columns from the training rows.
[med] Leave out `region`, `discount_pct`, the fees, `account_manager` and `campaign_code` unless a combination shows value, as none has signal alone.
[med] Recalibrate on the most recent complete months and take the base rate for the cost threshold from a known sample, not from this file.

[high] The model must beat the team's rule of 4 or fewer logins: on labelled rows it has 28.5% precision and 19.6% recall (37.2% precision without customers' earlier rows). The brief's bar is at least one third of churners with at least 40% precision.
[guess] The November step may also change which features matter later on. Check again on later months once the labels are in.

rows: staff, levels numbered on this page because the name suggests people

blocks.text: None of these was used in any measure of the target except `account_manager`, shown by numbered level only. Drop all of them before modelling.

items: Whether each feature is known at the moment of the prediction: there is no data dictionary, and six columns have no known source.
The true extract date: it is assumed from the last snapshot and supported only by the rates.
The cause of the November 2025 step, and whether it is a lasting change or seasonal, since the file holds one winter.
How rows were sampled, and whether the sample represents the active base.
The effect of past retention offers on these labels: the table does not show who received one.
Interactions between features: all strengths are one feature at a time.
Predictive power of a real model: nothing was trained.
`train.csv` and `test.csv` beyond their keys, and the other files in `data/`.
P-values treat rows as independent, and 1,500 customers have two rows, so read the intervals first. Those resample whole customers.
